title: ONAN HAD SEX WITH TAMAR—BUT REFUSED THE RESPONSIBILITY THAT CAME WITH IT
paragraphs:
ONAN HAD SEX WITH TAMAR—BUT REFUSED THE RESPONSIBILITY THAT CAME WITH IT
He wanted the intimacy without the obligation. He took what satisfied him while deliberately withholding what the relationship required. And buried inside one of Genesis’ most uncomfortable scandals is a warning about the terrifying difference between getting close to something sacred and actually surrendering to God.
There are Bible stories we sanitize because the details make us uncomfortable.
Genesis 38 refuses to let us do that.
There is a widow.
There is a dead husband.
There is a brother who knows what is expected of him.
There is sex.
There is deliberate refusal.
There is exploitation tangled inside family obligation.
And there is a God who sees what happens when someone accepts the privilege of a relationship while secretly rejecting the responsibility attached to it.
His name was Onan.
And perhaps the most disturbing thing about his story is not how foreign it feels.
It is how familiar the human heart behind it can become.
Because Onan did not simply walk away.
He went in.
That distinction matters.
After Tamar's husband Er died, Judah told his second son Onan:
“בֹּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיךָ וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ”
Bo el-eshet achikha, veyabbem otah, vehaqem zera le'achikha.
In context, the command means essentially:
Go to your brother's wife, fulfill the brother-in-law's duty toward her, and raise up offspring for your brother.
Genesis 38:8.
The Hebrew word וְיַבֵּם (veyabbem) comes from the root יבם (y-b-m), associated with performing the duty of a brother-in-law toward a childless brother's widow.

This family obligation appears before the Mosaic Law was given, so we should not anachronistically claim that Onan was violating the later written command of Deuteronomy 25. But when the Torah later formally regulates this institution, the same Hebrew root appears.
Deuteronomy 25:5 says:
“יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ ... וְיִבְּמָהּ”
Her brother-in-law was to take responsibility for the widow and perform the brother-in-law's duty.
And Deuteronomy explains part of what was at stake: the continuation of the deceased brother's name and household.
That takes us directly into Onan's heart.
Because Genesis does not leave us guessing about his motive.
“וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע”
Vayyeda Onan ki lo lo yihyeh hazzara.
“Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
Genesis 38:9.
There it is.
He knew.
This was not ignorance.
Not an accident.
Not confusion.
He understood the responsibility.
And he did not want its cost.
Yet he still went to Tamar.
Genesis describes his behavior with uncomfortable directness. Whenever he had relations with his brother's wife, he deliberately spilled his semen on the ground.
But do not stop reading there.
Because if you stop there, you can miss the explanation Scripture itself gives for what he was doing.
The Hebrew says:
“לְבִלְתִּי נְתָן־זֶרַע לְאָחִיו”
Levilti netan-zera le'achiv.
“So as not to give offspring to his brother.”
That final phrase is devastating.
Onan wanted what he could receive from the arrangement while deliberately sabotaging what he was supposed to give through it.
He accepted access.
Rejected obligation.
Participated physically.
Withheld intentionally.
And Tamar was left carrying the consequences.
She had already buried a husband.

Her future in that ancient household depended heavily upon family, offspring, protection, and the continuation of the line. Yet the man who had been called to help preserve that future repeatedly entered her bed while intentionally ensuring that the purpose entrusted to him would never be fulfilled.
Then Genesis says:
“וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה”
Vayyera be'enei YHWH asher asah.
“What he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”
Genesis 38:10.
Notice the wording.
What he did.
God saw not merely the outward act but the rebellion expressed through it.

This passage has often been reduced to a single debate about contraception or a particular sexual act. Christians have historically disagreed about some of the broader ethical implications drawn from Onan's behavior, and we should be careful not to make Genesis say less—or more—than it actually says.
What Genesis explicitly tells us is this:

Onan knew the offspring would not be counted as his brother's, and because of that, he deliberately prevented Tamar from conceiving whenever he went to her, specifically so that he would not provide offspring for his brother.
His selfish motive is written into the sentence.
And that makes this story far bigger than the mechanics of sex.
It is about a heart willing to receive what it wants while refusing what faithfulness requires.
And suddenly Onan's ancient bedroom becomes an uncomfortable mirror.
Because how many of us want the benefits of covenant without the responsibilities of covenant?
We want forgiveness without repentance.
Comfort without obedience.
Promises without surrender.
Resurrection without a cross.
A Savior who rescues us from hell, but not necessarily a Lord who tells us what to do with our bodies, money, relationships, ambitions, secrets, habits, sexuality, bitterness, pride, and future.
We want Jesus close enough to comfort us...
but sometimes not close enough to command us.
That is where this ancient scandal starts walking into our modern lives.
You can attend church and still resist Christ.
You can sing worship songs while protecting a secret addiction.
You can post Bible verses while refusing to forgive someone.
You can say, “God knows my heart,” while knowing perfectly well that your heart is precisely the battlefield you refuse to surrender.
You can love Christian encouragement while hating Christian correction.
You can want God's peace while resisting God's authority.
You can even want Jesus for what He gives without wanting Jesus for who He is.
And that is where grace must be understood correctly.
Grace is not God's permission to keep exploiting His mercy.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy toward sinners who could never rescue themselves.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing outside your rebellion saying, “Nothing needs to change.”
The Gospel is Jesus Christ entering the catastrophe of human sin, bearing judgment in the sinner's place, rising from the dead, forgiving those who come to Him, and giving them a new life.
Not purchased by our obedience.
Purchased by His blood.
And the grace that saves us does not leave us untouched.
This is why Jesus said:
“If you love me, keep my commandments.”
John 14:15.
Not:
“Keep My commandments so I might finally love you.”
That would turn grace into wages.
The order matters.
We love because He first loved us.
We obey because we belong to Him.
Repentance does not purchase salvation.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that has finally stopped defending its rebellion and runs toward the mercy of God.
And maybe this is where the story becomes painful.
Because perhaps you recognize something of Onan in yourself.
Not necessarily his particular sexual sin.
Something deeper.
Taking while withholding.
Receiving while resisting.
Wanting the blessing while refusing the burden of faithfulness.
Maybe you have been asking God to restore your marriage while secretly feeding the very behavior destroying it.
Maybe you have been praying for freedom while keeping private access to the thing enslaving you.
Maybe you want God to heal your heart, but you refuse to release the person you hate.
Maybe you want a godly relationship while repeatedly using people to soothe your loneliness.
Maybe you want financial blessing while refusing integrity when nobody is looking.
Maybe you want influence for Christ but cannot tolerate being unseen.
Maybe you want the crown...
but keep negotiating with the cross.
And here is where Genesis 38 becomes even more astonishing.
Because Tamar's story does not disappear into the scandal.
The family does not disappear.
Judah does not disappear.
The brokenness does not somehow prevent God from moving redemptive history forward.
Genesis 38 eventually records the birth of Perez through Tamar and Judah.
Then generations pass.
Names become genealogies.
Scandal becomes family history.
And when Matthew opens the New Testament and begins tracing the human ancestry of Jesus Christ, he does something remarkable.
He names Tamar.
“Tamar” appears in Matthew 1:3.
Think about that.
The Gospel of Matthew could have introduced Jesus with a polished genealogy that concealed every uncomfortable chapter.
Instead, Scripture carries Tamar's name forward.
Not because sin ceased to matter.
Not because everything that happened in Genesis 38 was righteous.
But because human scandal could not derail God's redemptive purpose.
Perez enters the line.
The generations continue.
David comes.
And ultimately, according to the flesh, the genealogy reaches Jesus Christ.

The Messiah enters a human family tree containing grief, sexual scandal, deception, failure, outsiders, kings, broken people, and stories most religious public-relations departments would probably prefer to hide.
God did not need a sanitized genealogy to send a spotless Savior.
Jesus was spotless.
The family history was not.
That is grace.
And maybe you need to hear that more than you realize.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your sin should not be renamed, excused, celebrated, or hidden.
It can be confessed.
It can be brought into the light.
It can be carried to Christ.
Because Jesus does not redeem us by pretending our sin was harmless.
He redeems sinners at enormous cost to Himself.
At the cross, mercy did not become cheap.
The Son of God paid.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
And the same Christ who forgives sinners also calls them out of darkness and into life.
So if this story exposed something hidden inside you, do not waste the conviction by turning it into temporary emotion.
Come to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary designed to make rebellion sound respectable.
No excuses.
“Jesus, I have wanted Your gifts while resisting Your rule.”
“Jesus, I have taken what I wanted and ignored whom I was hurting.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Change me.”
That prayer is not magic words.
But the Christ to whom a repentant sinner cries is mighty to save.
And if you have trusted Him, remember this too: conviction is not an invitation to despair. The answer to discovered sin is not to hide farther from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Walk differently.
And when you fall, do not make peace with the ground.
Get up and return to Christ.
Maybe somebody reading this has spent years believing that what happened in their family permanently disqualified them.
Look at Tamar's name in Matthew.
Maybe somebody thinks their sexual history has made them unusable.
Look toward Christ.
Maybe somebody has exploited another person's vulnerability and knows this article is describing more of their heart than they wanted exposed.
Do not defend it.
Repent.
Where restitution and confession to people you have harmed can rightly and safely be made, seek godly wisdom and take responsibility.
Grace is not hiding from responsibility.
Grace gives sinners somewhere to go when responsibility finally crushes their excuses.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes honesty begins when someone finally stops pretending.
If your spirit is exhausted and you need brothers and sisters in Christ to remember you in prayer, comment, “pray for me.”
And if God has been restoring places in you that you once thought were beyond repair, tell somebody what Christ has done.
Your testimony may become another wounded person's reason to look toward Jesus tonight.
Not because financial support proves that you love Jesus.
And certainly not because anyone can purchase favor with God.
The Gospel forbids that kind of manipulation.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, one legitimate expression of stewardship is voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel work so that biblical teaching can continue reaching people who desperately need Christ.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not miss the greater invitation.
You can share an article and still need Jesus.
You can own every Christian book ever printed and still need Jesus.
The product is not the point.
The page is not the point.
Gospel Warrior is not the point.
Jesus Christ is.
Onan's tragedy was that he knew what was required and still chose himself.
The Gospel announces something infinitely greater:
Christ knew exactly what our redemption would cost...
and still chose the cross.
Where selfish humanity says, “I will take, but I will not give,” Jesus says of His own life:
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.”
John 10:18.
Onan withheld.
Christ gave Himself.
We rebelled.
Christ obeyed.
We accumulated guilt.
Christ bore sin.
We deserved judgment.
Christ opened the door of mercy.
And death did not get the final word.
The tomb is empty.
The King is alive.
So the question left hanging over this ancient scandal is no longer merely what Onan did.
It is what you will do now that the light has reached you.
Will you keep negotiating?
Keep hiding?
Keep taking from God while resisting God?
Or will you finally open your hands and say:
“Jesus Christ, all of me belongs to You.”
Because the most dangerous place is not always far away from sacred things.
Sometimes it is close enough to touch them...
while the heart remains unsurrendered.
And the most beautiful truth is that even there, Christ still calls sinners to come home.
The scandal may explain where you have been—but when you surrender to Jesus, it does not get to decide where your story ends.
